source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Gage_2016_EpidemiologicEvidenceReview.pdf: Author's Accepted Manuscript (Elsevier cover page plus manuscript pages 1-20), all 21 PDF pages; pages cited as AM p. N with N = PDF page (one more than the manuscript's own number). Full text extracted with pdftotext -layout, also page by page; Table 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi (AM pp. 19-21). The version of record (Biol Psychiatry 2016;79:549-556) was not read.

claims.note: The Gage-attributed reading ('strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk') matches the abstract (AM p. 2). The review's conclusion goes further: a strong body of evidence that regular or heavy use increases the risk of persisting psychotic disorders (AM p. 13), so the claim, if anything, understates Gage's position; it does not overstate it. Gage also qualifies the claim's genetic reading: it judged shared genetic effects unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia variants explain little variance in cannabis use, and it cites a sibling-pair study (McGrath et al., 2010) in which the association held within sibling pairs. Both predate the Mendelian randomization and co-relative figures the claim uses, but the sibling-pair study is a family-based design pointing the other way that the claim does not mention. Gage describes the co-relative study (Giordano et al., 2015, ref. 26) qualitatively only, without numbers.

anchors.extracted: Authors' overall reading: the epidemiological evidence is strong enough to warrant a public-health message that cannabis use can increase the risk of psychotic disorders; further studies are needed on the size of the effect, the role of different types of cannabis and high-risk groups.

Authors state there is no doubt a public-health message that cannabis use is harmful is appropriate, while warning against overstating harms; conclusion: a strong body of epidemiological evidence supports the view that regular or heavy use increases the risk of psychotic disorders persisting beyond intoxication, with uncertainty inherent in observational evidence.

anchors.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Confounding, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Residual confounding would most likely inflate the association; studies adjusting for more confounders showed greater attenuation, 60-80% of the unadjusted estimate in the three most comprehensively adjusted studies (cited to ref. 9, Miettunen et al., 2008, a cross-sectional study; the figures match Moore et al.'s Table 1, ref. 10); early-life attachment, abuse and trauma rarely adjusted for.

anchors.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Confounding, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Shared genetic effects not adequately adjusted for but judged unlikely to explain the association, since schizophrenia variants explain little variance in cannabis use (ref. 24); a cross-sectional sibling-pair study found the association within sibling pairs; fixed-effects regression in CHDS changed little; a co-relative case-control study (ref. 26) found the association between cannabis disorder and schizophrenia substantially smaller with closer relatedness, from cousins to monozygotic twins, suggesting population estimates may be inflated by genetic and shared environmental effects (no numbers given).

anchors.locator: Addressing the uncertainty, 1st paragraph (AM p. 11) and 4th paragraph (AM p. 12)
anchors.extracted: Some uncertainty about causation will always remain with observational data; causal criteria are met, but associations meeting them have proved confounded when trials were run. Mendelian randomization could reduce confounding, but genetic variants that robustly predict cannabis use had not yet been identified.

claims.note: Gage-sourced figures check: Swedish conscripts 362 of 50,087 (Table 1, AM p. 19, rendered page), only men, schizophrenia by age 45 (AM p. 4); 362/50,087 = 7.2 per 1,000, same as the editors' 'about 7 in 1,000'; '1969' is in the title of ref. 12. ALSPAC 1.12 (0.76-1.65) and California HR 8.16 (5.08-13.12) as printed (AM pp. 4-5; Table 1 rounds to 8.2, 5.1-13.1); Zurich lost its weak association after adjustment (AM p. 5); about 2% lifetime risk with regular use, explicitly conditional on causality (AM p. 12). Omissions worth considering: (1) ALSPAC's association survived adjustment for pre-birth and childhood confounders and attenuated to the null only after adding cigarette and other illicit drug use, which the review flags as possible over-adjustment of correlated or mediating measures (AM p. 5); the claim names the adjustment but not the caveat. (2) Gage pooled the two newer cohorts with Moore's seven and reported an OR of 1.46 (1.24-1.72; I2 19%), which it calls very similar (AM p. 5); the claim's sentence that the association did not remain in two of the three newer cohorts reads more negatively than the review's own update. That update cannot be reproduced from the estimates the review prints, however: DerSimonian-Laird pooling of Moore's seven estimates (reproduced exactly: 1.41, 1.20-1.65, I2 19%) with Table 1's Zurich (unadjusted 1.77, 0.96-3.24) and ALSPAC (1.12, 0.76-1.65) gives 1.38 (1.20-1.59), I2 13% (second reader's calculation); the text says adjusted results from Zurich were used, but Table 1 says Zurich's adjusted results were not reported. Leaving the 1.46 out of the claim is therefore defensible, but the reason should be stated.

anchors.locator: Table 1, row 'Swedish cohort (12)' (AM p. 19); Evidence from cohort studies › Studies investigating psychotic disorder, 1st paragraph (AM p. 4)
anchors.extracted: Swedish conscripts: 50,087 men, 362 with the outcome (schizophrenia diagnosis); exposure cumulative use; linear-trend OR 1.2 (1.1-1.4); limitation 'only males included'. Text: dose-response between use by age 18 and incident schizophrenia by age 45; about threefold risk (95% CI 1.7-5.5) for more than 50 occasions by 18. Base rate 362/50,087 = 7.2 per 1,000 (second reader's calculation).

anchors.locator: Evidence from cohort studies, 1st paragraph and paragraphs on California (AM p. 4), Zurich and ALSPAC (AM p. 5); Table 1, rows Rossler, California and ALSPAC (AM p. 21)
anchors.extracted: Three cohorts published after Moore et al. (2007). California: hospital diagnosis of cannabis use disorder vs people admitted for appendicitis, HR 8.16 (5.08-13.12) for later hospitalisation for schizophrenia (Table 1: 41,670 people, 174 with outcome, 8.2, 5.1-13.1). Zurich (Rossler): weak evidence of an association with schizophrenia nuclear symptoms before but not after adjustment; Table 1: adjusted results not reported, unadjusted 1.77 (0.96-3.24). ALSPAC: cumulative use at 16 associated with psychotic experiences at 18 after adjustment for pre-birth and childhood confounders, attenuated to the null after further adjustment for cigarette and other illicit drug use, with the authors noting possible over-adjustment; Table 1: 1,756 people, 97 with outcome, 1.12 (0.76-1.65).

anchors.locator: Evidence from cohort studies, last paragraph
anchors.extracted: Summary of Moore et al.: about 40% higher risk (95% CI 20-65%) with any use, OR 2.1 (1.5-2.8) with heavier use, 2.6 (1.1-6.1) for psychotic disorder. Updated pooled OR adding Zurich and ALSPAC adjusted results (California left out for its extreme exposure): 1.46 (1.24-1.72), p < 0.001, I2 19%, described as very similar. Not reproducible from Table 1's printed estimates (second reader's pooling: 1.38, 1.20-1.59, I2 13%).

If the association is causal and of the size estimated by Moore et al., lifetime risk of schizophrenia with regular use would be about 2% (about 98% would not develop it); with a first-degree relative and an assumed twofold, multiplicative effect, about 20%; population attributable fraction 10-25% assuming causality; about 5,000 heavy-using men, and 10,000-15,000 women, would need to stop to prevent one case a year (from Hickman et al., 2009).

anchors.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Age of use, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Dunedin's stronger estimate for use by 15 rests on overlapping intervals and may reflect cumulative use; the Swedish conscripts showed no difference by age at first use when cumulative use was taken into account; no strong evidence that cannabis is more harmful to younger users, though animal data keep it an area of concern.

claims.note: Gage's position is reported accurately. Gage describes the skunk/hash contrast of Di Forti et al. (2015) in THC:CBD terms (skunk high, hash low), but no THC or CBD was measured there, which the claim states correctly.

anchors.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Strains of cannabis, 1st paragraph (continuing on AM p. 10)
anchors.extracted: A case-control study (ref. 48, Di Forti et al., 2015) found skunk-type (high THC:CBD) cannabis associated with a psychotic episode and hash (low THC:CBD) not; because studies from before skunk was widely used also found an association, it is too early to assume only skunk carries risk; longitudinal studies with accurate THC and CBD measures are needed and must address people selecting the extreme of use (heavy use earlier, stronger cannabis later) for reasons independently linked to psychosis risk (ref. 49).

anchors.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Strains of cannabis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Rising THC levels raise concern that older studies underestimate today's effects, but ecological evidence that psychosis risk has risen in young people exposed to higher-THC cannabis has not been examined.

anchors.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Misclassification bias
anchors.extracted: Cannabis types differ in cannabinoids; with no information on THC:CBD ratios, self-reported use does not reflect the compounds reaching the brain, and CBD may have antipsychotic effects; non-differential error would bias towards the null.

claims.note: Supported: Gage gives three of the reasons the claim attributes jointly to Gage and Hall (individuals' use and illness not linked, i.e. the ecological fallacy; confounders not accounted for; other competing risk factors that may have declined). Not in Gage: that even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and that changing diagnostic criteria, services and records could hide or create trends; these must rest on Hall (2015). Contradicted in part: the claim says the British general-practice study is 'known only through a 2008 government advisory report' (magnitude: 'third-hand'), but Gage cites it directly as a published paper: ref. 61, Frisher et al. (2009), Schizophrenia Research, on trends in diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005, among studies finding 'no change, or a decrease'. Also for the editor: two of Gage's four citations in this paragraph do not match their statements by title (ref. 58, Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2009, is on adult versus adolescent onset of smoking; ref. 60, Breslau et al., 2006, on race-ethnic differences in psychiatric disorder); ref. 59 (Boydell et al., 2003) covers south-east London 1965-1997.

anchors.locator: Evidence inconsistent with a causal relationship (single paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Cannabis use rose greatly from the 1960s without a matching rise in schizophrenia diagnoses, an argument against causation; some studies found rising incidence of psychotic outcomes (refs 58, 59), others no change or a decrease (refs 60, 61). The authors call such ecological evidence very weak: individuals using cannabis cannot be linked to those with psychosis, likely confounders are not accounted for, and other risk factors may have declined over the same period.

Ref. 59: Boydell et al. (2003), incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London 1965-1997. Ref. 61: Frisher et al. (2009), Schizophrenia Research, impact of cannabis use on trends in diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK 1996-2005 (the general-practice study, published). Refs 58 (Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2009, onset of smoking) and 60 (Breslau et al., 2006, race-ethnic differences in psychiatric disorder) do not match the statements they support by title.

anchors.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Strains of cannabis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ecological evidence that psychosis risk rose in young people exposed to higher-THC cannabis than earlier birth cohorts had not been examined (ref. 53).
